item.title: Polynomial Separation of a Shared Tensor Leg and Matrix Multiplication in Arbitrary Characteristic
item.description: arXiv:2610.18914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We improve the shared-leg separation construction in Proposition 3.1 of OpenAI, *An Upper Bound of $9/4$ for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent* (October 2, 2026). If $M$ tensor blocks have a common first space and independent matched sectors on their other two spaces, then $M+n-1$ copies of their matched sum degenerate to the full direct sum of the blocks, each tensored with an $n$-dimensional dot product. For $n=M$, this reduces the number of source copies from $5M$ to $2M-1$. The construction uses polynomial interpolation and truncated local substitution, with no roots of unity or factorial denominators. It works over every field containing enough distinct elements. We verify that the remaining spectral and discrete-growth arguments of the cited preprint are independent of characteristic. Over an algebraic closure, the replacement therefore gives $\omega\leq9/4$ in every characteristic.
item.dc:creator: Houxi L\"u

item.title: The Gap Between Average-Case and Worst-Case Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2610.19162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the average-case complexity of $\mathsf{NP}$ is a central goal in complexity theory and cryptography. A necessary milestone is to understand the corresponding average-case versus worst-case question for the polynomial hierarchy ($\mathsf{PH}$). In a celebrated result, Hirahara [Hir21] proved that if every distributional problem in $\mathsf{PH}$ is easy on average, then every language in $\mathsf{PH}$ admits worst-case algorithms running in time $2^{O(n/\log n)}$. Remarkably, although the statement of Hirahara's theorem makes no reference to meta-complexity, all known proofs appear to use time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity and its associated meta-computational problems in an essential way. We show that the reliance on techniques and perspectives from meta-complexity is not simply a coincidence. Building on previous work of Hirahara [Hir20] and on a recent result of Hu, Lu, and Oliveira [HLO25], we prove that relating the average-case and worst-case complexities of $\mathsf{PH}$ is in fact equivalent to a purely meta-computational implication: efficient algorithms for a standard gap version of $\mathsf{MINpKT}$ with $\mathsf{PH}$ oracle access imply efficient algorithms for a mild gap version. Crucially, in these promise problems the standard gap separates a YES instance with time bound $t$ from a NO instance with time bound $\mathsf{poly}(t)$, whereas the mild gap keeps the YES threshold $t$ and moves the NO threshold to $t+\mathsf{poly}(n)$. Together with prior work, this equivalence points to the study of gap reductions as a potentially promising route toward understanding the relation between average-case and worst-case complexity. We make progress by proving that the gap in running time can be eliminated in the average-case setting. Finally, we prove that in the worst-case setting any efficient reduction between the two problems must use nonrelativizing techniques.
item.dc:creator: Halley Goldberg, Jinqiao Hu, Zhenjian Lu, Jingyi Lyu, Igor C. Oliveira

item.title: Majority and Torus Polynomials: Bounded-Lift Lower Bounds and Explicit Constructions
item.description: arXiv:2610.19174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bhrushundi et al. (2019) introduced torus polynomial approximation as an approach to separating Majority from $ACC^0$. In this model, approximation is measured modulo integers. Krishan and Vishwanathan (2026) developed a duality framework for lower bounds and posed five open problems. We resolve two of these, concerning integer lifts and explicit polynomial approximations. An integer lift records the integer shifts that turn a torus approximation into an ordinary real approximation. We show that a degree-d torus polynomial approximating Majority with error at most 1/8 and lift contained in an interval of width $B$ must satisfy $d(B + 1) = \Omega(n)$. This rules out low-degree approximating polynomials with lifts in {-1, 0, 1}, answering their Open Problem 2. We also answer Open Problem 5 by giving, for every Boolean function on $n \geq 1$ variables, an explicit torus polynomial approximation of degree at most $n - 1$. Its error is optimal: zero when the accepting set has even cardinality and $2^{-n-1}$ otherwise. The results presented were discovered and formalized in Lean using GPT-6 Astra.
item.dc:creator: Saint Wesonga

item.title: A Simple Algorithm for Counting Solutions to Integer Programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.19200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of counting solutions to integer linear programming problems of the form $\{x \in \mathbb{Z}^n_{\geq 0} : Ax = b\}$ where $A \in \{-\Delta,\ldots,\Delta\}^{m \times n}$ and $b \in \mathbb{Z}^m$. We present an algorithm that counts solutions with $(n\Delta)^{m + o(1)}\! \cdot \log\lVert b\rVert$ arithmetic operations. This simplifies the algorithm of Gribanov and Malyshev, who considered the problem for the more general setting in which $A$ is $\Delta$-modular.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Dadush, Anita D\"urr, Thekla Hamm, Jonas Schmidt, Karol W\k{e}grzycki

item.title: Generalized Fibonacci gates are Frobenius algebras: a proof of Liu's conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.19230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liu introduced generalized Fibonacci gates on domains of size 3 and 4, proved that Holant problems built from them are tractable by a cut-and-merge algorithm, and conjectured that Fibonacci gates with matching polynomial-time algorithms exist on all higher domains. We extend the definition uniformly to every domain size $k$ and show that a family of domain-$k$ generalized Fibonacci gates is the same thing as a $k$-dimensional commutative Frobenius (equivalently, Artinian Gorenstein) algebra $A$ equipped with an orthonormal basis containing $1$. Under this dictionary Liu's parameter constraints are exactly associativity of $A$, a gate is an element $w\in A$, merging two gates is multiplication in $A$, and the Holant value of a connected graph $G$ is $\tau\bigl(h^{\,|E|-|V|+1}\prod_v w_v\bigr)$ for a fixed ``handle'' element $h\in A$. This proves Liu's conjecture for every $k$, with an algorithm whose cost is polynomial in $k$ as well as in the graph. We also give a closure criterion for linear recurrences of any depth (a balance condition implies closure, and is necessary when the unit is a combination of the colours), and we map the landscape: semisimple algebras are exactly Liu's orthogonal frames, smoothable algebras with nilpotents are collided frames, and families whose algebra is not smoothable (``frameless'' families) exist exactly when $k\ge 14$. Finally we show that every non-semisimple part of a family is invisible to the Holant on connected graphs with two or more independent cycles. This note states the results and sketches the proofs; the proofs of the main theorems are short and are given essentially in full.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Sterling

item.title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.19558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.
item.dc:creator: Kengo Hashimoto

item.title: Asymmetry and Complexity of Nondeterministic Computations
item.description: arXiv:2610.20188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry of Information (SoI) [ZL70] is a fundamental theorem of classical Kolmogorov complexity whose status for time-bounded computation is closely related to central open problems in complexity theory and cryptography. In a recent development, [HMO26] showed that SoI fails for $rKt$ complexity, namely in the setting of randomized computation. By contrast, many basic properties of Kolmogorov complexity are known to remain valid in the presence of nondeterminism [HLO26], suggesting that SoI may provide a fruitful structural principle for exploring the relative power of randomness and nondeterminism in computation. Our results reveal that the validity of SoI for nondeterministic computation, namely for $nKt$ complexity, is a subtle question connected to several frontiers. We show that symmetry of information holds on average for randomized extensions of $nKt$, while its worst case validity would imply breakthrough complexity separations. Although the standard cryptographic argument for asymmetry does not extend to the nondeterministic setting, we provide evidence that information remains asymmetric in nondeterministic computations. Among other results, we show that SoI would imply a collapse of exponential time classes to low levels of the polynomial hierarchy. Then, building on the work of [Hir22b, GK22, KK26, HMO26], we develop a general framework connecting symmetry of information, meta-complexity, and explicit constructions in the nondeterministic setting. More precisely, we prove that suitable formulations of these three notions are quantitatively equivalent. We apply different aspects of this correspondence to make progress on complexity lower bounds and on the failure of SoI for nondeterministic computation. These consequences are unconditional and provide some of the strongest known lower bounds in meta-complexity.
item.dc:creator: Halley Goldberg, Jinqiao Hu, Zhenjian Lu, Jingyi Lyu, Igor C. Oliveira

item.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.20492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the number of exact matrix-vector queries needed to sample a centered $d$-dimensional Gaussian with condition number at most $\kappa$ to total variation error $\varepsilon$. The best known algorithm uses $O(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\frac{d}{\varepsilon})\})$ queries, while the known lower bounds do not grow as $\varepsilon\to0$ and match this bound only for $\kappa\le d^{1/5-\delta}$ at constant accuracy. We introduce a construction based on a hidden determinant sign and prove a lower bound of $\Omega\!\left(\min\left\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right)\right\}\right)$ uniformly for all $d\ge1$, $\kappa\ge4$, and $0<\varepsilon\le\tfrac{1}{16}$. This bound matches the known upper bound up to constant factors whenever $\kappa\le d^{2-\delta}$ for fixed $\delta\in(0,2)$, or $\varepsilon\le d^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. We also extend a recent fixed-spectrum construction with a hidden eigenbasis from $\kappa=2$ to $2\le\kappa\le d^{1-\delta}$, for any fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$. This gives an $\Omega_\delta(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound at constant accuracy that holds even when the spectrum of the precision matrix is known to the algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Huanjian Zhou, Taiji Suzuki

item.title: A Factor-Two Lower Bound for Complementing Two-Way Deterministic Finite Automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.18897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For every $n\ge22$, we construct a language over a fixed three-letter alphabet whose two-way deterministic state complexity is $n$ and whose complement has state complexity $2n$. Acceptance is at the left endmarker, and infinite computations reject. The lower bound holds for arbitrary deterministic recognizers. The proof uses the group of transformations induced by the witness to constrain the behavior of a smaller recognizer, then derives a contradiction from a permutation query problem. A matching halting complement follows from a $2n$-state construction for sources whose destination states determine the direction of each transition. Splitting states by incoming direction gives a $2n+2b$ upper bound for general sources, where $b$ counts states entered in both directions. In the acceptance-anywhere model of Geffert, Mereghetti, and Pighizzini, the same family has exact complexities $N$ and $2N-1$ for every $N\ge23$.
item.dc:creator: Sudais Arif

item.title: Semi-Linearity and Generalized Stratified Semi-Linearity beyond Context-Free Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.19562v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parikh's famous theorem relates to the semi-linearity of context-free languages. We seek for expanding the scope of the semi-linear property from context-free languages to languages beyond them. Of those languages, this work focuses on the languages that are particularly recognized by one-way nondeterministic depth-k storage automata under a natural restriction of frozen blank sensitivity. Those languages (which are called $k$-storable languages) have been already proven to satisfy a natural generalization of the well-known pumping lemmas for regular and context-free languages. The semi-linearity of k-storable languages generalizes Parikh's theorem on the semi-linearity of context-free languages. As for bounded languages, Ginsburg and Spanier's well-known theorem characterizes context-free languages in terms of stratified semi-linearity. This notion is further generalized and is used to characterize the k-storable languages as well. Such a generalization is interesting in its own right. This helps us take an abstract treatment of k-storable languages without relying on "machines". Our results strengthen the belief that those languages are "natural" generalizations of context-free languages.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Geometric Kernel Diversity: An Axiomatic Diversity Measure in Euclidean Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.19570v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantifying the diversity of a set of objects is a fundamental problem in machine learning and statistics. Mironov and Prokhorenkova (2025) recently showed that three axioms-monotonicity, uniqueness, and continuity-are crucial for a reliable diversity measure and that none of the standard metrics in the literature satisfy all three. They also constructed two measures that do satisfy the axioms, but both are NP-hard to compute, leaving open the question of whether efficient axiomatic diversity measures can exist. We study a Euclidean-restricted version of this question. We introduce Geometric Kernel Diversity (GKD), which associates a radial kernel solid with each point and measures the volume of their union. We show that canonical GKD satisfies all three Mironov-Prokhorenkova axioms on Euclidean-realizable inputs. For canonical GKD, we give exact polynomial-time algorithms in dimensions $d \le 3$. In arbitrary dimensions, we give a randomized algorithm that returns a $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$-approximation with probability at least $1-\delta$ in time $O \left(\frac{nd}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}\right)$ for $n$ points. The axiomatic guarantee applies to exact canonical GKD; the randomized algorithm approximates this deterministic quantity. We further show that the two diversity measures of Mironov and Prokhorenkova (2025) remain NP-hard on Euclidean-realizable inputs and, unless $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$, admit no FPRAS even on this restricted domain.
item.dc:creator: Ditbul Ban, Younghun Roh, Julian Shun, Vihan Lakshman

item.title: Full AFLs Closed under Nested Iterated $k$-Variate Substitution and Depth-k Storage Automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.19584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Greibach and Ginsburg (1969) studied abstract families of languages or AFLs. A full AFL is a class of languages closed under the following operations: homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, intersection with regular languages, union, concatenation, and Kleene star. Greibach (1970) used a restricted substitution, called nested iterated substitution, to introduce the notion of super AFLs, which are full AFLs that are further closed under nested iterated substitution. The smallest super AFL was shown to be the class of all context-free languages. From this fact, we focus on Greibach's limited, univariable application of nested iterated substitution and further generalize it into k-variate. This introduces the notion of nested iterated $k$-variate substitution whose definition does not rely on "machines". Recently, a "two-tape" version of Hibbard's (1967) rewriting systems, which were later reformulated by Pighizzini and Pisoni (2014) as k-limited automata with "single" input/work tapes, has been studied under the name of depth-k storage automata. This work unearths a few characteristics of the languages recognized by those automata under a restriction known as frozen blank sensitivity in terms of full AFLs and nested iterated k-variate substitution. This will promote a further abstract treatment of those languages.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu

item.title: On the Complexity of Linear Programs with Parametric Constraint Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.20422v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While sensitivity analysis for linear programs with parametric right- hand side vectors is well established, cases involving parametric constraint matrices remain less explored. To address this gap, we investigate linear programs where the constraint matrix depends linearly on a scalar parameter. Our goal is to compute the minimum and maximum optimal values of these parametric linear programs within a fixed parameter range. This corresponds to solving two bilevel programs. We show that both decision versions of these optimization problems are NP-complete by proving both NP-hardness and membership in NP. We additionally identify three sufficient conditions on the parametric matrix under which the bilevel programs are no longer NP-hard. We introduce a reformulation for both problems, together with a Farkas-based certificate for the lower-level feasibility condition, and compare the execution time for solving them on standard benchmark instances. The experiments highlight a practical dichotomy. Although both bilevel optimizations are NP-hard, computing the parameter value corresponding to the minimum of the linear program is fast, whereas computing the value corresponding to the maximum is not. We relate this asymmetry to the parametric equality constraints, whose free dual variables leave the relaxation of the maximum reformulation unbounded.
item.dc:creator: Laurie Boveroux, Margarida Carvalho, Andrea Lodi, Quentin Louveaux

item.title: Conormal Lower Bounds for Determinantal Complexity: Fermat Slices, Tight Bounds, and a Ceiling
item.description: arXiv:2606.15970v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The determinantal complexity of a polynomial $f$ is the smallest size of a matrix of affine linear forms whose determinant is $f$; the border version only asks for determinants converging to $f$. The polar method bounds these quantities from below by comparing an invariant of the hypersurface $V(f)$, such as the degree of its dual variety, with the number of solutions of a polynomial system built from a determinantal representation of $f$. We determine how far the method reaches. Lower bounds: if $f$ has a linear restriction to a form of degree $d$ in $N$ variables with smooth projective zero set, then the border determinantal complexity of $f$ is at least $(N-1)(d-1)/(4e)$. Setting the off-diagonal host entries to zero turns every homomorphism polynomial $\hom_{F,q}$ with a connected pattern $F$ into a Fermat polynomial, which gives the bound $(q-1)(|E(F)|-1)/(4e)$. For the VBP-complete path family $W_q$ this is tight: the border determinantal complexity of $W_q$ is $\Theta(q^3)$. The same argument gives cubic bounds for natural VP- and VNP-complete families, and a bound in terms of the codimension of the singular locus of $V(f)$. A ceiling: the method, together with every refinement in a precisely defined class, cannot prove a lower bound larger than $O(dN)$ for any polynomial of degree $d$ in $N$ variables. The proof computes the solution count exactly, as the degree of the dual of a generic determinantal hypersurface, and shows that every characteristic-cycle invariant of a hypersurface of degree $d$ is at most $8(d-1)^{N-1}+8N$. For the $n\times n$ permanent the ceiling is $O(n^3)$; for the power sum $x_1^N+\dots+x_N^N$ it is $(1+o(1))N^2/(4e)$, matching the known lower bound.
item.dc:creator: Karthik Sheshadri

item.title: Lettericity Is NP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2609.28023v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The lettericity of a graph $G$ is the smallest size of a set $\Sigma$ such that there exist $w_1, \ldots, w_{|V(G)|} \in \Sigma$ and a so-called decoder $D \subseteq \Sigma^2$ for which $G$ is isomorphic to the letter graph $(\{1, \ldots, |V(G)|\}, \{ij : 1 \le i < j \le |V(G)|, w_iw_j \in D\})$. It took around two decades of the study of lettericity for, in the simpler case of paths, a closed-form expression for its lettericity to be derived; this suggests that the question of whether the lettericity of an arbitrary graph can be computed in polynomial time is nontrivial. Indeed, this question has been raised repeatedly as an open problem in recent literature. We solve this problem by showing that the lettericity problem on arbitrary graphs is NP-complete. We also show that each of the natural ways in which a single part of a structure $(\Sigma, w_1, \ldots, w_{|V(G)|}, D)$ witnessing the lettericity could be constrained corresponds to an NP-complete problem, which resolves an additional three open problems from the literature; in particular, we show that the coloring extension, word extension, and decoder extension problems are NP-complete. Additionally, we use the reduction in the NP-completeness proof to give a lower bound on algorithms for lettericity under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH): unless the ETH is false, there cannot exist a deterministic algorithm to decide whether the lettericity of an $n$-vertex graph is at most $k$ in time $2^{o(n)}$, even when $n = 6k$. Finally, we complement the known result that Lettericity is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the standard parameter $k$ by providing a fixed-parameter algorithm with respect to the dual parameterization by $n-k$ running in $2^{\mathcal{O}((n-k)^2)} + \mathcal{O}(n)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Henning Fernau, Samuel German, Kevin Mann, Nils Morawietz

item.title: The No Endmarker Theorem for One-Way Probabilistic Pushdown Automata
item.description: arXiv:2111.02688v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In various models of one-way pushdown automata, the explicit use of two designated endmarkers on a read-once input tape has proven to be extremely useful for making a conscious, final decision on the acceptance/rejection of each input word immediately after reading the right endmarker. With no endmarkers, by contrast, a machine must constantly stay in either accepting or rejecting states at any moment since it never notices the end of the input word. This situation, however, helps us analyze the behavior of the machine whose tape head makes the consecutive moves on all prefixes of a given extremely long input word. Since those two machine formulations have their own advantages, it is natural to ask whether the endmarkers are truly necessary to correctly recognize languages. In the deterministic and nondeterministic models, it is well-known that the endmarkers are removable without changing the acceptance/rejection criteria of each input word. This paper demonstrates that, for a more general model of one-way probabilistic pushdown automata, the endmarkers are always removable. This is proven by employing probabilistic transformations from an "endmarker" machine to an equivalent "no-endmarker" machine at the cost of double exponential stack-state complexity without compromising its error probability. By setting the machine's error probability appropriately, our proof also provides an alternative proof to both the deterministic and the nondeterministic models as well.
item.dc:creator: Tomoyuki Yamakami

item.title: Computational Aspects of the Trace Norm Contraction Coefficient
item.description: arXiv:2507.16737v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that approximating the trace norm contraction coefficient of a quantum channel within a constant factor is NP-hard. Equivalently, this shows that determining the optimal success probability for encoding a bit in a quantum system undergoing noise is NP-hard. This contrasts with the classical analogue of this problem that can clearly be solved efficiently. We also establish the NP-hardness of deciding if the contraction coefficient is equal to 1, i.e., the channel can perfectly preserve a bit. As a consequence, deciding if a non-commutative graph has an independence number of at least 2 is NP-hard. In addition, we establish a converging hierarchy of semidefinite programming upper bounds on the contraction coefficient.
item.dc:creator: Idris Delsol, Omar Fawzi, Jan Kochanowski, Akshay Ramachandran

item.title: Fundamental Limitations of QAOA on Constrained Problems and a Route to Exponential Enhancement
item.description: arXiv:2511.17259v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the feasibility limitations of generic QAOA for permutation-constrained optimization, where valid configurations occupy an exponentially small fraction of the Boolean hypercube. Using random edge-cost TSP/ATSP ensembles, we establish high-probability bounds showing that optimized generic QAOA retains exponentially small feasible probability over specified parameter domains. At depth one, the bound holds uniformly over all mixer angles and a cost-angle grid that may be exponentially large in n^2. The analysis combines Walsh-Fourier/Krawtchouk estimates, which suppress low- and high-degree contributions, with transition-feature collision bounds controlling objective-dependent interference. Complementary cost-angle averaging, fourth-moment estimates, and light-cone analysis characterize energy-fibre coherence, typical-angle concentration, and constraint-correlation geometry. We compare generic QAOA with a constraint-enhanced kernel (CE-QAOA) initialized in a product one-hot subspace and evolved with a block-local XY mixer. For N = n^2 binary variables, CE-QAOA attains feasible probability at least n!/n^n at every depth, yielding an exp[Omega(n^2)] advantage over optimized generic QAOA at depth one with high probability. For linked cost-angle schedules with independently optimized mixer angles, the generic feasibility obstruction and exponential CE-QAOA separation extend throughout linear-depth windows p <= alpha*n, for fixed alpha > 0. These parameter-uniform bounds also imply exponential raw-sample requirements for adaptive feasible sampling within the prescribed domains.
item.dc:creator: Chinonso Onah, Kristel Michielsen

item.title: Gray Codes With Constant Delay and Constant Auxiliary Space
item.description: arXiv:2602.11791v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give the first two algorithms to enumerate all binary words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ (like Gray codes) while ensuring that the delay and the auxiliary space is independent from $\ell$, i.e., constant time for each word, and constant memory in addition to the $\ell$ bits storing the current word. Our algorithms are given in two new computational models: tape machines and deque machines. We also study more restricted models, queue machines and stack machines, and show that they cannot enumerate all binary words with constant auxiliary space, even with unrestricted delay. A tape machine is a Turing machine that stores the current binary word on a single working tape of length $\ell$ (which never increases), using no other tape. The machine has a single head and must edit its tape to reach all possible words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$, and output them (in unit time, by entering special output states), with no duplicates. Hence a tape machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition (up to the head position). We construct a tape machine that achieves this task with constant delay between consecutive outputs, so that the machine implements a so-called skew-tolerant quasi-Gray code. We then construct a more involved tape machine that implements a Gray code. A deque machine stores the current binary word on a double-ended queue of length $\ell$, and stores a constant-size internal state. It works as a tape machine, except that it modifies the content of the deque by performing push and pop operations on the endpoints. Hence again a deque machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition. We construct deque machines that enumerate all words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ with constant-delay. The main technical challenge in this model is to correctly detect when enumeration has finished.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Amarilli, Claire David, Nadime Francis, Victor Marsault, Mika\"el Monet, Yann Strozecki

item.title: The power of unentanglement without destructive interference
item.description: arXiv:2604.27886v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Stoquasticity, originating in sign-problem-free physical systems, gives rise to $\sf StoqMA$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (2006), a quantum-inspired intermediate class between $\sf MA$ and $\sf AM$. Unentanglement similarly gives rise to ${\sf QMA}(2)$, introduced by Kobayashi, Matsumoto, and Yamakami (CJTCS 2009), which generalizes $\sf QMA$ to two unentangled proofs and still has only the trivial $\sf NEXP$ upper bound. In this work, we initiate a systematic study of the power of unentanglement without destructive interference via ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$, the class of unentangled stoquastic Merlin--Arthur proof systems. Beyond its complexity-theoretic interest, ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$ is connected to the optimality of non-negative tensor optimization algorithms. We highlight: 1. ${\sf NP} \subseteq {\sf StoqMA}(2)$ with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$-qubit proofs and completenes $1-2^{-{\rm polylog}(n)}$. Conversely, the Sum-of-Squares algorithm of Barak, Kelner, and Steurer (STOC 2014) gives an exponential-time upper bound for ${\sf StoqMA}(2)$. Our tightened analysis shows the optimality of our protocol and the BKS algorithm under ETH. 2. For logarithmic-size proofs, ${\sf NP} \subseteq {\sf StoqMA}(2)_{\log}$ with completeness $1-O(n^{-2})$ and vanishing gap, while ${\sf StoqMA}(2)_{\log} \subseteq {\sf MA}$. Consequently, quantum-inspired randomness enables exponentially shorter unentangled proofs even under the assumption ${\sf MA}={\sf NP}$. 3. For ${\sf StoqMA}(2)_1$, the parameter dependence in the general ETH-optimal time bound can be exponentially improved, or the bound achieved simultaneously with polynomial space. Our lower bounds are obtained by stoquastizing the short-proof ${\sf QMA}(2)$ protocols using distribution testing techniques. Our upper bounds for the nearly perfect completeness case are proved via our rectangular closure testing framework.
item.dc:creator: Yupan Liu, Pei Wu

item.title: Algorithmic Unverifiability of Safety for Fixed and Recursively Self-Improving Systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.28639v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing impossibility results for AI verification concern a fixed system. Self-modifying systems (agents that rewrite their own code, recursive self-improvement loops) raise a different question: can a safety property that holds now be certified, in advance, to keep holding after the system rewrites itself? We model one step of self-modification as a total computable transformation of code, and preservation as 'safe now and safe after the step'. If the transformation depends only on behaviour, preservation is Rice's theorem one level up; if it reads the code, as self-modification does, preservation is no longer semantic, yet at least as hard as the halting problem, by the same s-m-n reduction carried out inside a class of behaviourally identical programs. One step is never harder than the property; persistence along the whole trajectory can be one arithmetical level higher. No tower of supervisors lowers the problem; every total supervisor errs on a set of systems it cannot locate. Every faithful scheme certifying on finite behavioural evidence admits, for properties not settled by any finite set of inputs, an evolution trace it certifies at every stage while the property is violated. Statically, we record the classical limits (Rice, Goedel, Trakhtenbrot) and add the resource face: over succinctly described finite environments, verifying a policy against an adversary is coNP-complete and synthesising one PSPACE-complete. These limits do not say self-modifying systems are unsafe; they locate where algorithmic guarantees break, at the expressivity a general system needs: Turing-completeness and unrestricted self-modification. What survives is exact: a monitor detects the first violation of a safety property, and no sound procedure certifies all safe systems; certification requires restricting rewrites by design; and a frozen reference keeps the question well posed.
item.dc:creator: Jose Pascual Gumbau Mezquita

item.title: Near-Optimal Online Metric Matching on $\Delta$-ary HST
item.description: arXiv:2609.25292v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the online metric matching problem, we have $n$ servers with known locations in some metric space. Requests arrive one-by-one at certain locations, and upon arrival a request must be matched to a server that was not matched to a previous request. The goal is to minimize the matching cost. For randomized algorithms with an oblivious adversary, the best known competitive ratio is obtained by embedding the metric space into an HST, and then solving the problem in the setting where the metric space is defined by the HST. Bansal et al. (Algorithmica, 2014) introduced a framework for online metric matching where one develops an algorithm in a restricted reassignment model, and then transforms this into a true online algorithm. Using this framework, they obtained an expected competitive ratio of $O(\log n)$ for HSTs; this also gives the best known competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 n)$ for general metrics. In this paper, we revisit this framework with the aim of developing new algorithms. For HSTs where each node has at most $\Delta$ children, we develop an algorithm via this framework with an expected competitive ratio of $O((\log\log \Delta) \cdot \log \Delta)$. In particular, this ratio is independent of $n$, the number of servers/requests. It is near-optimal, as the expected competitive ratio of any algorithm is $\Omega(\log \Delta)$.
item.dc:creator: Parth Gor, Sourya Roy, Kasturi Varadarajan

item.title: QMA(2) with Limited Shared Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2609.39668v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$, two computationally unbounded provers submit unentangled quantum witnesses to a polynomial-time quantum verifier. We ask whether allowing limited shared entanglement between the two provers changes the power of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$. To this end, we formalize $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)$, a variant in which the provers initially share $h$ EPR pairs, as suggested by Aaronson, Beigi, Drucker, Fefferman, and Shor (ToC~2009). We show that polynomially many shared EPR pairs give the provers no cheating advantage: $\mathsf{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)$ for $h=\operatorname{poly}(n)$. For logarithmically many pairs, the power of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ remains unchanged, strengthening this inclusion to $\mathsf{QMA}(2)=\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)$ for $h=O(\log n)$. Finally, we introduce a variant that also allows classical communication between the provers when preparing the witnesses. This setting is particularly revealing for logarithmic-size witnesses: assuming $\mathsf{NP}\nsubseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, we show that superlogarithmically many shared EPR pairs strictly reduce the model's computational power.
item.dc:creator: Alex Della Schiava, Ranitha Mataraarachchi
